rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The singular āyah reading treats the whole affair of Joseph as one lesson and sign, supported by the verse saying their story contains a lesson.
rows.anchor: فالحجة لمن وحد أنه جعل أمر يوسف عليه السلام كله عبرة وآية

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The plural āyāt reading makes each of Joseph’s actions a sign; the written tāʾ form also made this reading easy to write.
rows.anchor: جعل كل فعل من أفعاله آية فجمع لذلك وسهله عليه كتبها في السواد بالتاء

rows.speaker: الفراء
rows.claim: Al-Farrāʾ derives āyah on the pattern faʿlah, with the underlying form ayah.
rows.anchor: وزن آية عند الفراء فعلة أية

rows.speaker: الكسائي
rows.claim: Al-Kisāʾī analyzes āyah as fāʿilah, with an underlying doubled yāʾ.
rows.anchor: وعند الكسائي فاعلة آيية

rows.speaker: سيبويه
rows.claim: Sībawayh analyzes āyah as faʿlah, also with an underlying doubled yāʾ.
rows.anchor: وعند سيبويه فعلة أيية

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The ending of mubīn is read with either ḍamma or kasra on the tanwīn; the source refers readers to its earlier discussion in al-Nisāʾ for the argument.
rows.anchor: يقرا بضم التنوين وكسره وقد ذكرت علته في النساء

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The word ruʾyā is read with tafkhīm or imālah; imālah signals that its final alif is feminine because it corresponds in form to tāʾ.
rows.anchor: يقرا بالتفخيم والإمالة فالحجة لمن فخم أنه أتى به على الأصل

rows.speaker: الكسائي
rows.claim: Al-Kisāʾī reportedly makes imālah in this ruʾyā but opens the word in ruʾyāka; this is mistaken if meant to distinguish case, but sound if showing both permissible dialects.
rows.anchor: وروي عن الكسائي أنه أمال هذه وفتح قوله

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The singular ghiyābah means the particular place where Joseph fell and what concealed him; one body occupied one place.
rows.anchor: أنه أراد موضع وقوعه فيه وما غيبه منه لأنه جسم واحد شغل مكانا واحدا

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The plural ghiyābāt refers to the well’s darkness and its surrounding places, treating each part as a hiding place.
rows.anchor: أنه أراد ظلم البئر ونواحيه فجعل كل مكان في غيابة

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Reading the verbs with nūn makes the brothers the subject: they will roam and play together.
rows.anchor: لمن قرأهما بالنون أنه أخبر بذلك عن جماعتهم

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Reading the verbs with yāʾ makes Joseph alone their subject.
rows.anchor: لمن قرأه بالياء أنه أخبر بذلك عن يوسف دون إخوته

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The sukūn reading derives yartaʿ from ratiʿa, roaming freely across the land for play and amusement.
rows.anchor: لمن أسكن العين أنه أخذه من رتع يرتع

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The kasra reading derives the verb from grazing; its original yāʾ was deleted because the jussive answers the brothers’ request to send Joseph.
rows.anchor: أخذه من الرعى واصله إثبات الياء فيه فحذفها دلالة على الجزم لأنه جواب للطلب

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The brothers could play because they were not prophets at that time.
rows.anchor: كيف يلعبون وهم أنبياء فقل لم يكونوا إذ ذاك أنبياء

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The hamza-retaining reading of dhiʾb follows the word’s origin in tadhʾubu, a wind that blows from every direction; dropping the silent hamza eases pronunciation.
rows.anchor: فالحجة لمن همز أنه اتى به على أصله لأنه مأخوذ من تذؤب الريح

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Adding the final alif and opening yāʾ in yā bushrā makes the cry an attribution to the speaker, like yā ḥasratī and yā waylatī.
rows.anchor: أراد الإضافة إلى نفسه كقوله يا حسرتي ويا ويلتي

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Dropping that alif and making yāʾ still treats Bushrā as a boy’s name, derived from glad tidings on the faʿlā pattern.
rows.anchor: جعله اسم غلام مأخوذ من البشارة مبني على وزن فعلى

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Imālah in bushrā is prompted by the rāʾ; its true articulation is toward yāʾ, so kasra brings the sound closer.
rows.anchor: الإمالة فيه فلمكان الراء وحقيقتها على الياء فأشار بالكسر إلى الراء

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Opening hāʾ and rounding tāʾ in hayta laka compares it to ḥaythu.
rows.anchor: فتح الهاء وضم التاء أنه شبهه ب حيث

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Kasra on hāʾ and fatḥa on tāʾ reflect the neighboring yāʾ.
rows.anchor: ومن كسر الهاء وفتح التاء فإنما كسرها لمكان الياء

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Opening both vowels compares the hāʾ to hallumma and opens tāʾ after a still yāʾ, as in ayna, layta, and kayfa.
rows.anchor: جعله مثل الهاء في هلم وفتح التاء لأنها جاءت بعد الياء الساكنة

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: With fatḥa, mukhlaṣīn is a passive participle: God purified them; with kasra, mukhliṣīn is an active participle, one who is sincere.
rows.anchor: فالحجة لمن فتح أنه أراد أسم المفعول به من قولك أخلصهم الله

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The final alif in ḥāshā may be retained in connected and paused speech from ḥāshā yuḥāshī, or omitted in both because fatḥa suffices and the consonant skeleton omits it.
rows.anchor: بإثبات الألف في آخره وصلا ووقفا وبحذفها في الوجهين معا

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Here ḥāshā means seeking refuge in God; grammarians also explain it as an exception meaning I exempt, and al-Nābighah’s verse witnesses the verb.
rows.anchor: ومعناها ها هنا معاذ الله وهي عند النحويين بمعنى أستثني واستشهدوا بقول النابغة

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Sukūn in daʾban marks a verbal noun, while fatḥa marks a noun; the opening vowel may also have been reduced for ease in a guttural environment.
rows.anchor: فالحجة لمن أسكن أنه أراد المصدر والحجة لمن فتح أنه أراد الاسم

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Daʾb means continuous perseverance, adherence, or habitual practice; al-Kumayt’s line uses it for persistent travel.
rows.anchor: والدأب معناه المداومة على الشيء وملازمته والعادة قال الكميت

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The author prefers sukūn in daʾban because the same word is consistently read that way in the phrase about Pharaoh’s people.
rows.anchor: والاختيار السكون لإجماعها عليه في قوله

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The forms khayra ḥifẓan and khayra ḥāfiẓan reflect an underlying possessive construction; ḥifẓan is a distinguishing accusative, while ḥāfiẓan is a circumstantial accusative and may also be distinguishing.
rows.anchor: والأصل فيهما والله خيركم حفظا وحافظا فنصب قوله حفظا على التمييز

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: In Zayd afrahu ʿabd, the genitive makes the servant the one who is a better horse; in afrahu ʿabdan, Zayd is compared as an owner of a better servant or horse than others.
rows.anchor: إذا خفضوا فالفاره هو العبد وإنما مدحته في ذاته وإذا نصبوا فالعبد غير زيد

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: In nuḥī ilayhim, yāʾ makes the verb passive, whereas nūn makes it God’s first-person report about Himself.
rows.anchor: يقرا بالياء والنون وفتح الحاء مع الياء وكسرها مع النون

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Reading tattakhidhū with yāʾ reports the command about the Children of Israel in the third person; tāʾ directly addresses them.
rows.anchor: فالحجة لمن قرأه بالياء أنه رده على بني إسرائيل

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The fatḥa reading of the hamza in li-yasūʾū makes the verb part of the promised punishment; the ḍamma plus wāw makes the servants themselves subject.
rows.anchor: أنه جعله فعلا للوعد وللعذاب والحجة لمن قرأه بالضم أنه جعله فعلا للعباد

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The yāʾ readings in the paired purpose clauses match the following verbs li-yadkhulū and li-yutabirū; nūn instead has God report the actions of Himself.
rows.anchor: والقراءة بالياء في هذين الوجهين فأما النون فإخبار عن الله عز وجل

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Faces stands for faces and bodies, as wajh can stand for God Himself in the verse saying all things perish except His face; the purpose verb is subjunctive after lām.
rows.anchor: وخص الوجوه وهو يريد الوجوه والأبدان

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: With light qāf and still lām, the book itself meets the person; with doubled qāf and open lām, the verb is passive and the pronoun refers to the book.
rows.anchor: بتخفيف القاف وسكون اللام وبتشديدها وفتح اللام

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Doubled mīm in amarnā means granting rule and authority; the light form means commanding the affluent to obey, after which they rebel.
rows.anchor: بالتشديد والتخفيف فالحجة لمن شدد أنه أراد به الإمارة والولاية

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The idiom amara Banū Fulān can mean they became numerous; Allāh āmarahum means He increased and blessed them.
rows.anchor: وأما قول العرب أمر بنو فلان فمعناه كثروا والله آمرهم أي كثرهم وبارك فيهم

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Af with tanwīn is an indefinite expression for something vile; the kasra without tanwīn may break the meeting of two still consonants, and fatḥa without tanwīn is another transmitted form.
rows.anchor: يقرا بالكسر منونا وغير منون وبالفتح من غير تنوين فالحجة لمن نون

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The word af expresses vexation and stands by euphemism for every kind of ugly or offensive speech.
rows.anchor: وهي كلمة تقال عند الضجر ولو علم الله تعالى أوجز منها في ترك العقوق

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Its vowel is not inflectional but eases two adjacent still sounds; unlike particles such as rabb and thumma, af allows varied vowels because it conveys prohibition, like the imperative ih.
rows.anchor: لأن حركتها ليست بحركة إعراب إنما هي لالتقاء الساكنين

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Ibn al-Anbārī adds two forms, with a light fāʾ and with the fāʾ still.
rows.anchor: وزاد ابن الأنباري أف بتخفيف الفاء وبإسكانها

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The poet’s imperative fa-ghuḍḍ al-ṭarf shows that the final consonant can take ḍamma by assimilation, fatḥa for two still sounds, or kasra by the usual easing of adjacent still sounds.
rows.anchor: كما قال فغض الطرف إنك من نمير فلا كعبا بلغت ولا كلابا

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: With the alif, yablughāni refers back to both parents and drops the dual marker nūn before the emphatic nūn; without it, one parent is the subject and al-kibara is the object.
rows.anchor: أنه جعلها ضميرا للوالدين وكناية عنهما لتقدمهما وأسقط النون التي هي علامة الإعراب

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The emphatic nūn follows imma because that conditional particle commonly takes an emphatic nūn on its verb.
rows.anchor: وأتى بالنون الشديدة لدخول إما على الفعل لأنها قلما تدخل على فعل

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Aḥaduhumā can be parsed as an appositive to the verb’s alif, the subject of an implicit repeated verb, or an answer to an implied question about who reaches old age.
rows.anchor: أحدهما أنه يرتفع بدلا من الألف التي في الفعل والثاني أنه يرتفع بتجديد فعل مضمر

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Parents receive special emphasis in old age because movement and service become harder; the proverb about the eagle says its grown chick feeds it when it can no longer fly.
rows.anchor: لأنهما عند الكبر يثقل عليهما الاضطراب والخدمة فخصا بالبر فيه لذلك

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The comparison says a person is more dutiful to parents than an eagle, whose fledgling feeds it when age prevents flight.
rows.anchor: فلان أبر بوالديه من النسر لأن أباه إذا كبر ولم ينهض للطيران

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The yāʾ form of la-yusrif refers back to the guardian without directly addressing him; the tāʾ form addresses the guardian and those present.
rows.anchor: فمن قرأه بالياء رده على الولي لأنه غير مقصود بمواجهة الخطاب

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Isrāf in killing means killing ten for one, or killing someone other than the murderer because that person is prominent while the murderer is obscure.
rows.anchor: ومعنى الإسراف أن تقتل عشرة بواحد أو يقتل غير القاتل لشرفه في قومه

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Qisṭās has both qāf vowels as eloquent forms; ḍamma is more common in the Hijaz. The word means scales and came from Greek, whose loanwords Arabic adapts flexibly.
rows.anchor: وهما لغتان فصيحتان والضم أكثر لأنه لغة أهل الحجاز ومعناه الميزان

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: With fatḥa on the hamza, sayyiʾa is one bad deed and is opposed to good; with ḍamma and possessive hāʾ, it is an annexed form supported by Ubayy’s reading.
rows.anchor: والحجة لمن قرأه بالإضافة قوله مكروها ولو أراد السيئة

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Every act God forbids is bad and disliked, with nothing praiseworthy in it; the verse about mixing good and bad deeds supports this reading.
rows.anchor: أن كل ما نهى الله عز وجل عنه سيئ مكروه ليس فيه مستحسن

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: A singular form after kull may express the word’s grammatical form, while a plural expresses its collective meaning.
rows.anchor: لفظ كل يقتضي الجمع فلم لم يؤت بعده بجمع

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Liyadhdhakkarū is read with doubled or light dhāl; the author says its argument was given earlier.
rows.anchor: بالتشديد والتخفيف وقد ذكر القول فيه آنفا

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The two occurrences of ʿammā yaqūlūn are read with yāʾ or tāʾ; the author refers to an earlier discussion of the rationale.
rows.anchor: يقرأن بالتاء والياء فالحجة لمن قرأه يقولون في الموضعين

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The tāʾ reading of tusabbiḥu is supported by Ubayy’s past-tense sabbaḥat; the yāʾ reading treats the heavens as a small plural that Arabic may make masculine.
rows.anchor: والحجة لمن قرأ تسبح بالتاء قراءة أبي سبحت له السموات والحجة لمن قرأه بالياء

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The author says a small plural precedes a large one and masculine precedes feminine, so agreement can follow the earlier form; examples include al-ashhur and niswah.
rows.anchor: والعلة في ذلك أن الجمع القليل قبل الكثير والتذكير قبل التأنيث

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The reading of aʾidhā kunnā ʿiẓāman wa-rufātan is deferred to an earlier discussion in al-Aʿrāf.
rows.anchor: مذكور في الأعراف والعلل فيه

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: In akhkhartanī, retaining yāʾ follows the original form; deleting it relies on its kasra to signal it.
rows.anchor: يقرأبإثبات الياء وحذفها فالحجة لمن أثبتها أنه أتى به على الأصل

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Although in normally governs a future or past, lam of emphasis seeks a raised verb while in requires jussive; the past is used because its form displays neither ending.
rows.anchor: فلما جمعوا بينهما لم يجز اجتماع الرفع والجزم في فعل واحد فعدلوا عن المستقبل

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Sukūn on the jīm in rajl is the regular plural of rāجل; kasra is caused by the neighboring lām’s kasra and is supported by the poet’s ḥajal.
rows.anchor: فالحجة لمن أسكن أنه أتى بالجمع على حقه لأنه جمع راجل والحجة لمن كسر

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The verbs yakhsifa, yursila, and yughrika have nūn or yāʾ: nūn is God speaking of Himself, while yāʾ has the Prophet report from his Lord.
rows.anchor: يقرأكله بالنون والياء فالحجة لمن قرأه بالنون أنه جعله من إخبار الله

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The two aʿmā forms may both be imālah, both tafkhīm, or imālah only on the first; imālah marks words with underlying yāʾ, while tafkhīm follows their surface alif.
rows.anchor: يقرآن بالإمالة والتفخيم معا وبإمالة الأول وتفخيم الثاني

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The first aʿmā describes the person as blind in the worldly blessings just described; the second says he will be blind and further astray in the next life.
rows.anchor: ومن كان فيما وصفنا من نعيم الدنيا أعمى فهو في نعيم الآخرة أعمى وأضل

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: A mixed imālah reading treats the first word as a plain adjective and the second as comparative: more blind in the next life than in this one.
rows.anchor: أنه جعل الأول صفة والثاني بمنزلة أفعل منك ومعناه ومن كان في هذه أعمى

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Both khilāfaka forms mean after you, not opposition; a poem uses khilāf to mean what remains after a group leaves.
rows.anchor: ومعناهما بعدك وهما لغتان وليس من المخالفة قال الشاعر نؤي أقام خلاف الحي

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Opening nūn and hamza in naʾā preserves the root’s original form, naʾā, on faʿala; the word means to move away.
rows.anchor: أنه أتى بالكلمة على أصلها لأنها في حقيقة اللفظ نأي على وزن فعل

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Kasra on both nūn and hamza signals the underlying yāʾ by imālah; neighboring vowels draw each other toward kasra, as in shaʿīr and baʿīr.
rows.anchor: أنه أمال الياء للدلالة عليها فكسر لها الهمزة ليقر بها منها بالمجاورة

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Opening nūn but making hamza kasra keeps nūn original and brings hamza toward the neighboring yāʾ; all these forms mean distance, and the noun is al-naʾy.
rows.anchor: والحجة لمن فتح النون أنه بقاها على أصلها وكسر الهمزة لمجاورة الياء

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Postponing hamza with a lengthened vowel derives nāʾa yanūʾu, to rise while bearing a heavy load; its original wāw became alif, as in the verse about a band of men.
rows.anchor: أنه أراد معنى ناء ينوء إذا نهض بثقل مطيقا لحمله

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The doubled form tafajjara derives from fajjara and is supported by the cognate tafjīran; the light form comes from fajara, splitting ground and making water flow.
rows.anchor: فالحجة لمن شدد أنه أخذه من فجر يفجر ودليله قوله تفجيرا

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Kisafan with fatḥa is the plural of kisfah, a piece; with sukūn it resembles a verbal noun such as ʿilm or ḥilm.
rows.anchor: فالحجة لمن فتح أنه أراد به جمع كسفة

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Idʿū is read with ḍamma or kasra; the author refers readers to the earlier discussion in al-Baqarah.
rows.anchor: يقرأبالضم والكسر وقد ذكر في البقرة

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Al-muhtadī is read with its final yāʾ retained or omitted; the author refers to al-Aʿrāf for the argument.
rows.anchor: يقرأبإثبات الياء وحذفها وقد ذكر في الأعراف

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: In min ladunhu, the nūn may be still and the pronoun’s ḍamma realized as wāw, preserving the word’s full form, as in minhu and ʿanhu.
rows.anchor: لمن أسكن النون وألحق ضمة الهاء واوا أنه أتى بالكلمة على أصلها

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: A shortened vowel on the pronoun avoids a heavy wāw at the end of a noun after a rounded vowel.
rows.anchor: لمن أختلس حركة الهاء أنه اكتفى بالضمة من الواو لثقلها في أواخر الأسماء

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Another reading hints at ḍamma on dāl, then kasras nūn and hāʾ and adds yāʾ; the hint avoids a heavy ḍamma, while kasra resolves two still sounds.
rows.anchor: أشار إلى حركة الدال بالضمة وكسر النون والهاء وألحقها ياء

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Ladun means ʿinda, is an indeclinable locative, and normally governs genitive; unlike ʿinda, it cannot extend to distant presence or figurative knowledge, with ladun ghudwata exceptional in taking accusative.
rows.anchor: ولدن في جميع أحوالها بمعنى عند لا يقع عليها إعراب وهي ظرف مكاني

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Mirfaq with kasra on mīm derives from irtifāq, finding rest; with fatḥa it refers to the hand; the author also allows both as eloquent dialect forms.
rows.anchor: بكسر الميم وفتح الفاء وبفتح الميم وكسر الفاء فالحجة لمن كسر الميم

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The yāʾ form of lam yakun separates the verb from its noun and treats feminine agreement as nonactual, supported by the plural yansurūnahu; tāʾ is supported by visible feminine marking and collective use.
rows.anchor: يقرأبالياء والتاء فالحجة لمن قرأه بالياء ما ذكرناه آنفا من الفصل بين الفعل والاسم

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Ṭāʾifah and fiʾah can each be singular or plural.
rows.anchor: والطائفة والفئة يكونان واحدا وجمعا

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The spelling of miʾah adds alif to distinguish it from minhu in writing; fiʾah has no such ambiguity and keeps its original spelling.
rows.anchor: إنما زيدت الألف في قولك أخذ مائة درهم لئلا يلتبس في الخط

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Wilāyah with fatḥa is a verbal noun from waliya; kasra derives it from wālā or wālaytuhu, with both also accepted as dialect forms.
rows.anchor: يقرأ بفتح الواو وكسرها فالحجة لمن فتح أنه جعله مصدرا من قولك ولى

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Raising al-ḥaqq makes it an adjective of wilāyah, supported by Ubayy’s word order; lowering it makes it an adjective of God, supported by the verse naming God their true master.
rows.anchor: يقرأبالرفع والخفض فالحجة لمن رفع أنه جعله وصفا

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: ʿAbd Allāh’s reading places al-ḥaqq after Allāh as a new assertion, and al-ḥaqq can mean God, truth in speech, rightful kingship, or certainty after doubt.
rows.anchor: وقرأه عبد الله هنالك الولاية لله وهو الحق فالحق الله عز وجل والحق صدق الحديث

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: A syntactic accusative is also possible if an implied verb is understood: aḥaqqa al-ḥaqq, meaning He made the truth true.
rows.anchor: ويجوز في النحو والنصب بإضمار فعل على المصدر معناه أحق الحق

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The tāʾ reading with rafʿ makes the mountains the passive subject, with feminine agreement for a nonhuman plural; the verse saying they were made a mirage supports it.
rows.anchor: بالتاء والرفع وبالنون والنصب فالحجة لمن قرأه بالتاء أنه جعل الفعل لما لم يسم فاعله

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The nūn reading makes God the speaker and takes al-jibāl as object; the nearby first-person verbs ḥasharnāhum and lam nughadir support this agreement.
rows.anchor: لمن قرأه بالنون أنه جعله من إخبار الله تعالى عن نفسه ونصب الجبال

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Yawm is either an object of an implied udhkur addressed to Muhammad or a time adverb for the reward with God on the day the mountains move.
rows.anchor: ويوم منصوب بإضمار فعل معناه واذكر يا محمد يوم نسير الجبال

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Bārizah means the earth is exposed and nothing is hidden; alternatively, what it contains of treasure and the dead emerges.
rows.anchor: ومعنى قوله بارزة أي ظاهرة لا يستتر منها شيء لاستوائها

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Yaqūlu with yāʾ reports the command through the Prophet from God; nūn makes God speak in the first person.
rows.anchor: يقرأبالياء والنون فالحجة لمن قرأه بالياء أنه

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Qubulan with both vowels rounded is plural of qabīl and means group by group; with kasra on qāf and fatḥa on bāʾ it means visibly and face to face.
rows.anchor: يقرأ بضم القاف والباء وبكسرها وفتح الباء فالحجة لمن ضم أنه

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Some linguists say qabīlah means a tribe descended from a father and qabīl means a group, citing the demand to bring God and the angels qabilan.
rows.anchor: وقال بعض أهل اللغة القبيلة بنوأب والقبيل الجماعة واستدل بقوله

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: A poem uses qabīl for the opposing host, which is certain to be first to prevail when the two armies meet.
rows.anchor: وبقول الشاعر جوانح قد أيقن أن قبيلهم إذا ما التقى الجمعان

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The hāʾ in ansānihi may be rounded in its original form or kasra by proximity to yāʾ; al-Kisāʾī makes imālah in the preceding alif to indicate its underlying yāʾ.
rows.anchor: يقرأبضم الهاء وكسرها مختلستين فالحجة لمن ضم أنه أتى بلفظ الهاء

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Rushdan with two ḍammas follows the neighboring vowel pattern, as in al-ruʿb and al-suḥt.
rows.anchor: يقرأ بضمتين وفتحتين وبضم الراء وإسكان الشين فالحجة لمن قرأه بضمتين

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Fatḥa on both letters means uprightness in religion; ḍamma on rāʾ and sukūn on shīn means sound judgment in wealth and maturity, as in the verse about testing orphans.
rows.anchor: لمن قرأه بفتحتين أنه أراد به الصلاح في الدين والحجة لمن قرأه بضم الراء

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Opening both mīm and lām in mahلك is a verbal noun from halakū; kasra on lām makes it the time or place of their destruction, like the sunset’s location.
rows.anchor: بفتح الميم وضمها وبفتح اللام وكسرها فالحجة لمن فتحها أنه جعله مصدرا

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Ḍamma on mīm with fatḥa on lām derives from ahlakahum and means their destruction; the source compares it with madkhal in the verse about entering truthfully.
rows.anchor: لمن قرأه بضم الميم وفتح اللام أنه جعله مصدرا من قولهم أهلكهم الله مهلكا

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: In li-tughriqa ahlahā, ḍamma on tāʾ makes Moses directly responsible and takes the people as object; fatḥa on yāʾ makes the people the subject of the drowning.
rows.anchor: يقرأ بالتاء مضمومة ونصب الأهل وبالياء مفتوحة ورفع الأهل

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: One answer is that Moses knew more than Khidr about what conveys God's proof to people, apart from this matter; another is that he sought knowledge he lacked despite his other knowledge.
rows.anchor: أحدها أن يكون موسى أعلم من الخضر بما يؤدي عن الله تعالى إلى خلقه

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: A third answer, for those who consider Khidr a prophet, is that God may give one prophet more knowledge than another.
rows.anchor: يمكن أن يكون الله تعالى أعطى نبيا من العلم أكثر مما أعطى غيره

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Raḥman with ḍamma or sukūn on ḥāʾ are both dialect forms; the word means mercy, affection, or closeness of kin.
rows.anchor: يقرأ بضم الحاء وإسكانها وهما لغتان كالعمر

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Fa-ittabaʿa with hamzat waṣl and doubled tāʾ follows iftaʿala from ittabaʿa; hamzat qaṭʿ and still tāʾ derives from atbaʿa, meaning to catch up with someone.
rows.anchor: يقرآن بألف الوصل وتشديد التاء وبألف القطع وإسكان التاء

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The first form means traveling in someone’s tracks, the second catching up; the verse about a shooting star following another witnesses the latter. Sabab here means road, elsewhere a rope or kinship.
rows.anchor: معنى اتبعه بألف الوصل سرت في أثره ومعنى أتبعته بألف القطع لحقته

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The hamzated ḥamiʾah reading means a black muddy spring, perhaps water mixed with mud; the nonhamzated ḥāmiyah means a hot spring, as in the verse describing blazing fire.
rows.anchor: يقرأ بغير ألف وبالهمزة وبالألف من غير همز فالحجة لمن قرأها

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: With rafʿ and annexation, jazāʾ is the subject and is annexed to al-ḥusnā; the predicate is that it belongs to him. Al-ḥusnā means goodness, good deeds, or gracious reward.
rows.anchor: فالحجة لمن رفع وأضاف أنه رفع الجزاء بالابتداء واضافه إلى الحسنى فتم بالإضافة اسما

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The accusative can put the verbal noun in place of a circumstantial phrase, meaning the garden is granted as reward; alternatively it is a weak distinguishing accusative.
rows.anchor: لمن قرأه بالنصب أنه أراد به وضع المصدر في موضع الحال

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The distinguishing accusative is weak because it is fronted without a conjugated verb; a cited poem is offered in support by some grammarians.
rows.anchor: وفيه ضعف لأن التمييز يقبح تقديمه سيما إذا لم يأت معه فعل متصرف

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Sadd with ḍamma means a barrier in the natural or divinely made sense; fatḥa means a human-built barrier, a distinction some extend to God's work versus people's work.
rows.anchor: يقرأ بضم السين وفتحها فالحجة لمن ضم أنه جعله من السد في المعين

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Ḍamma on yāʾ in yafqahūn derives from afqaha and means they can scarcely make others understand; an object is omitted. Fatḥa derives from faqaha, understanding what one hears.
rows.anchor: يقرأ بضم الياء وكسر القاف وبفتحهما فالحجة لمن ضم الياء أنه

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The hamzated Yaʾjūj and Maʾjūj may derive from the blaze of fire or harsh, briny water, making them Arabic forms on a verbal pattern and proper tribal names.
rows.anchor: يقرآن بالهمز وتركه فالحجة همز أنه أخذه من أجيج النار

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: If the names are foreign, they have no Arabic derivation; the nonhamzated reading treats them like Tālut, Jālūt, Hārūt, and Mārūt.
rows.anchor: فأما من جعله أعجميا فليس له اشتقاق والحجة لمن لم يهمز أنه جعله عجميا

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Kharjan with alif means a recurring levy or tribute collected by a ruler; without alif it means payment or compensation. The later kharāj keeps alif by consensus and rasm.
rows.anchor: يقرأ بإثبات الألف وطرحها ها هنا وفي المؤمنين فالحجة لمن أثبتها

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Assimilating the two nūns in makkannī eases and shortens the form, analyzing mā as relative and khayr as its predicate; keeping them distinct preserves the original radical and augmentative nūns.
rows.anchor: يقرأ بنون شديدة وبنونين ظاهرتين فالحجة لمن أدغم أنه أراد التخفيف والإيجاز

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Ṣadafayn with both ḍammas follows the base form and vowel harmony; opening both is lighter and treats ṣadaf as singular, supported by a report about the Prophet passing a leaning ṣadaf.
rows.anchor: يقرأ بضم الصاد والدال وفتحهما وبفتح الصاد وإسكان الدال

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: A reading with fatḥa on ṣād and sukūn on dāl treats ṣadaf as the name of the mountain itself; a rajaz line refers to the two mountain slopes.
rows.anchor: لمن أسكن الدال أنه جعله اسما للجبل بذاته غير مثنى وانشد الراجز

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Ātūnī with madd means give me the iron; with qaṣr it means come. The author prefers the meaning give because coming would take the preposition bi-, as in the verse about bringing Jacob’s family.
rows.anchor: يقرأ بالمد والقصر فالحجة لمن مد أنه جعله من الإعطاء

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The light form of istaṭāʿū is the general reading; doubled ṭāʾ is reported from Ḥamzah and criticized for combining two still consonants without a long vowel.
rows.anchor: يقرأبالتخفيف إلا ما روي عن حمزة من تشديد الطاء وقد عيب بذلك

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The author defends the doubled form by analogy to other readings that assimilate across still consonants; speakers also treat still sounds alike and may imagine movement or stillness by analogy.
rows.anchor: عليه عيب لأن القراء قد قرأوا بالتشديد قوله

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The author prefers the consensus form, representing istaṭāʿū with deletion of tāʾ to avoid adjacent letters with close points of articulation and the resulting assimilation.
rows.anchor: والاختيار ما عليه الإجماع لأنه يراد به استطاعوا فتحذف التاء كراهية لاجتماع

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The reading and arguments for dakkā are deferred to the earlier discussion in al-Aʿrāf.
rows.anchor: مذكور العلل في سورة الأعراف

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The yāʾ and tāʾ readings of tanfada are noted, with their arguments deferred to an earlier discussion.
rows.anchor: يقرأ بالياء والتاء وقد ذكرت حجته آنفا في غير موضع

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Opening all the disconnected letters follows their basic vowel; the letters take fatḥa to distinguish spellings from ordinary nouns, verbs, and particles that undergo imālah.
rows.anchor: يقرأبفتح جميع حروفه وبإمالتها وبين الإمالة والفتح

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Imālah separates the hāʾ of attention from the spelled letter hāʾ and distinguishes a vocative use from spelling.
rows.anchor: أنه فرق بين هاء التنبيه وهاء الهجاء وبين ما إذا كانت نداء وإذا كانت هجاء

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The between-reading form compromises between the two pronunciations and takes the nearer of the two dialects.
rows.anchor: لمن قرأهن بين بين أنه عدل بين اللفظين وأخذ بأقرب اللغتين

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Some vowels are imālah and others full because readers avoid a run of consecutive kasras or fatḥas; Arabic also genders, lengthens, shortens, and tilts letter names.
rows.anchor: لمن أمال بعضا وفخم بعضا أنه كره توالي الكسرات أو الفتحات

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Spelled letters are lengthened by count: two-letter names take a medium length and three-letter names a greater length.
rows.anchor: فما كان منها على حرفين مد مدا وسطا وما كان على ثلاثة أحرف مد فوق ذلك

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: One explanation is that God swears by the alphabet because its letters compose His names, using letters from the beginnings of the sūrahs.
rows.anchor: وقيل في معناهن إن الله تعالى أقسم بحروف المعجم لأنها أصل لتأليف أسمائه

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Other reported explanations call the disconnected letters a sign for the sūrah or a divine secret entrusted to the Prophet.
rows.anchor: وقيل هي شعار للسورة وقيل هي سر الله تعالى عند نبيه

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Another explanation assigns each letter a divine name: kāf from kāfī, hāʾ from hādī, ʿayn from ʿalīm, and ṣād from ṣādiq.
rows.anchor: وقيل كل حرف مها نائب عن اسم من أسماء الله عز وجل فالكاف من كاف

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The reading ṣād dhikr may preserve clear pronunciation by origin or assimilate because the two consonants are close.
rows.anchor: يقرأباظهار على الأصل وبالإدغام للمقاربة بين الحرفين

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The two-word phrase dhikri raḥmati may be assimilated by removing rāʾ’s vowel to match adjacent sounds, or pronounced clearly because a vowel and word boundary block assimilation.
rows.anchor: يقرأبالإدغام وطرح الحركة من الراء لمجانسة الحرفين

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Sukūn on the yāʾ in min warāʾī accommodates the long, heavy word with its hamza; Ibn Kathīr instead lengthens an open yāʾ to avoid a still possessive yāʾ before a kasra hamza.
rows.anchor: يقرأبإسكان الياء لطول الاسم وثقله بالهمز إلا ما روي عن ابن كثير

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Jussive yarithnī answers the request for a child, with the implicit condition if You grant me one; raised yarithnī is a relative clause describing the indefinite walī.
rows.anchor: يقرأبالجزم والرفع فالحجة لمن جزم أنه جعله

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Raised yarithnī may instead function as a circumstantial participle, equivalent to wālithan; the author calls this analysis somewhat weak because its antecedent is indefinite.
rows.anchor: ولو قيل إنه إنما جاز الرفع في قوله يرثني وما أشبهه لأنه حال حل محل اسم الفاعل

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Wa-yarith is raised or jussive according to the same two analyses already given for yarithnī at the start of the passage.
rows.anchor: يقرأ بالرفع والجزم عطفا على ما تقدم من الوجهين في أول الكلام

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Kasra in ʿitiyyan and similar forms follows the neighboring yāʾ and avoids a shift from ḍamma; ḍamma preserves their original fuʿūl pattern, where wāw became doubled yāʾ.
rows.anchor: يقرأ بالكسر والضم وما شاكله من قوله

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The singular forms underlying these plurals contain wāw from verbs such as ʿatā and jathā; it changes to yāʾ after kasra, and the heavier plural follows that change.
rows.anchor: الأصل في الواحد من هذا الجمع عاتو وجاثو لأنه من يعتو

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: ʿAtaw in the cited phrase retains wāw because it is a light verbal noun; the corresponding plural is heavier and follows the changed singular.
rows.anchor: فأما قوله عتوا فإنما صح بالواو لأنه مصدر والمصدر يجري مجرى الاسم الواحد

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The source rejects a parallel kasra in maḍiyyan: it is a verbal noun from maḍā yamḍī, not a plural of māḍin, so the plural analogy does not apply.
rows.anchor: هذا لا يلزم لأنه مصدر والفعل منه مضى يمضي مضاء ومضيا

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Khalaqtuka with tāʾ and khalaqnā with nūn plus alif both report God’s action, linked respectively to the preceding speech and to wa-ḥanānan min ladunnā.
rows.anchor: يقرا بالتاء وبالنون والألف فالحجة لمن قرأه بالتاء أنه رده

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Lam takun shayʾan means Zechariah had not been a visible, created, existent thing to creatures, although he was already a thing in God's knowledge.
rows.anchor: فقل معناه ولم تك شيئا مرئيا مخلوقا موجودا عند المخلوقين

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The name Yaḥyā is explained as God bringing life from two infertile parents who had passed ninety and despaired of having a child.
rows.anchor: وإنما سمي يحيى لأنه حيي من عقمين قد نيفا على التسعين ويئسا من الولد

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Samiyyan may mean no one before bore the same name, or that no child had been born to his parents before him; the later question about a namesake allows both senses.
rows.anchor: قيل لم يسم باسمه غيره وقيل لم يولد لأبويه ولد قبله

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Li-yahaba with yāʾ makes Gabriel report what God will grant; li-ahaba with hamza has Gabriel speaking of his own role as the one who blew by God’s command.
rows.anchor: يقرأبالياء والهمزة فالحجة لمن قرأه بالياء أنه جعله من إخبار جبريل

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Nasyan with fatḥa is a verbal noun from nasiya; with kasra it means a discarded thing that has been thrown away and forgotten.
rows.anchor: يقرأ بفتح النون وكسرها فالحجة لمن فتح أنه أراد المصدر

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: A poem describes a modest woman as seeking a thing she dropped, so that she may learn its story; tabtulu means she relates and tells truthfully.
rows.anchor: والعرب تقول هذا الشيء لقى ونسي ومنه قول الشاعر يصف امرأة بالحياء والخفر

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: With fatḥa on mīm and tāʾ, man taḥtahā is the person below Mary, identified as Jesus; the locative phrase is an adverbial object for the place where the caller is.
rows.anchor: لمن فتح أنه جعله اسم عيسى وفتح التاء لأنه ظرف مكاني متضمن لجثة

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: With kasra on mīm and tāʾ, min is a preposition governing the place below her, which is conceived as a container in which the action occurs.
rows.anchor: لمن كسر الميم والتاء أنه جعلها حرفا خافضا للظرف لأنه اسم للموضوع

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The caller is Gabriel; min can mark an origin, a partitive, or an emphatic addition.
rows.anchor: والمراد بالنداء جبريل فأما مواقع من في الكلام فتقع ابتداء غاية

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Tāsāqaṭ with shadda comes from tatasaqaṭ after deleting the second tāʾ and assimilating it into sīn; the light form deletes a tāʾ, since speakers ease adjacent matching consonants by assimilation or omission.
rows.anchor: يقرأ بالتشديد والتخفيف فالحجة لمن شدد أنه أراد تتساقط

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Wa-awṣānī has imālah or tafkhīm; the author refers to earlier examples for the argument.
rows.anchor: يقرأ بالتفخيم والإمالة وقد ذكر في أمثاله من الاحتجاج

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Qawla al-ḥaqq in the accusative is a verbal noun, as in saying something truthfully; nominative makes it an apposition to Jesus or supplies an implicit repeated predicate.
rows.anchor: يقرأ بالرفع والنصب فالحجة لمن نصب أنه وجهه إلى نصب المصدر

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Jesus is called God's word because he came to be by God's word kun; he is His spirit because he was a mercy to those who believed and were saved.
rows.anchor: فعيسى كلمة الله لانه بكلمته كان وقوله لأنه بقوله كن تكون وروحه لأنه كان رحمة

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Opening hamza in wa-anna joins this statement to wa-awṣānī biṣ-ṣalāh; kasra starts a new sentence, supported by Ubayy’s reading without the wāw.
rows.anchor: يقرأبفتح الهمزة وكسرها فالحجة لمن فتحها أنه رد الكلام بالواو

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The readings of a-wa-lā yadhdhakkaru with a doubled or still k are referred to earlier examples.
rows.anchor: يقرأ بتشديد الكاف وفتح الذال وبضم الكاف وإسكان الذال

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Mukhlasan with fatḥa means one purified by God; with kasra it means one who is sincere, following the same argument given for mukhliṣīn earlier.
rows.anchor: يقرأ بفتح اللام وكسرها والحجة فيه كالحجة في المخلصين

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Hal taʿlamu may be assimilated because the sounds are close, or pronounced clearly according to the original separation of its consonants.
rows.anchor: يقرأ بالإدغام للمقاربة وبالإظهار على الأصل وانفصال الحرفين

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Nunajjī with doubling derives from najjā; the light form derives from anjā.
rows.anchor: يقرأ بالتشديد من نجى وبالتخفيف من أنجى
